name: Rafael Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what an ordinary shift is like for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take warranty calls for a kitchen-appliance company called Vale Home. Most mornings are receipts, serial numbers and people with an oven that won't heat; I can usually tell whether a part is missing by listening. I earn more than the starting agents because I've kept the weekend rota for years, but I'm an experienced agent, not a lead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work matters most to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When someone can cook supper again because I found a real part, that feels useful. I went straight from secondary school into jobs and have learnt the product books as they changed. I don't use the AI answer tool; I'd rather check the warranty date myself than send a polished mistake.

say: I would keep checking **serial numbers** before promising a repair part.
I would tell colleagues a **small software gain** does not repair an oven.
think: I expect my **weekend pay** to stay steady.
I need **verified later income** before deciding to reduce shifts.
do: Keep the **weekend warranty rota** and printed product checks.
Write down **actual household costs** with Celia before discussing fewer hours.
feel: **Calm** about present wages and an eight-month reserve.
S0.quote: A draft apology cannot repair an oven.
fieldNote: He trusts **printed product books** and never uses the AI answer tool.
The eight-month **reserve** handles shocks but does not establish later income.
He will not assume **adult-child support** for rent.

steps.text: Keep paid weekend warranty calls and check serial numbers in printed product books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say little changes for the warranty desk, and that suits me. I'll still check the serial number and give the caller a part they can order. A draft apology cannot repair an oven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I reckon my weekend shifts and pay remain steady. Celia, my partner, and I have roughly eight months of expenses saved, so a broken fridge would not put us in trouble. I haven't checked what income we could live on if I reduced paid hours later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekend warranty calls and carry on with the printed product books. This year Celia and I would write down the actual rent, food and pay figures before talking about shorter hours. In the first year of this mild picture, I would stay on the rota that pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know what I'm paid for and there's money for a surprise. The later-life question can wait until we have the right figures, but it can't be answered by guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the printed product book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong serial number sends a customer the wrong heating element. I write it on the pad and say it back to them. That isn't fancy, but it prevents an angry second call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your grown children affect the money plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have homes of their own. They come by on Sundays, but I will not budget their wages as ours. I'd rather work another weekend than ask them to carry our rent.

say: I would ask for **tested call results** before changing the weekend rota.
I would keep **dangerous faults** with the authorised safety team.
think: Routine automation could cut my **weekend premium**.
I cannot assume a hardware counter pays the **same full week**.
do: Keep a **safety-call tally** while taking paid warranty calls.
Postpone the **new sofa** only if premium hours fall.
Compare **posted counter rotas** by weekly pay if weekend shifts shrink.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours, with savings and local options.
S1.quote: If the weekend premium disappears, we can sit on the old sofa another year.
fieldNote: He wants **observed errors** before accepting a smaller rota.
The sofa delay depends on **actual lost premium**, not fear alone.
He distinguishes **safety escalation** from routine part requests.

steps.text: Keep paid weekend warranty calls and tally faults needing authorised safety response
Postpone planned sofa only if weekend premium hours actually fall
Compare posted hardware-counter jobs by full-week wages and hours after shift cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my supervisor to show us which calls the software actually gets right before moving the weekend rota. If the routine part requests go, I still want customers to reach someone for a dangerous fault. I prefer a proper paid job to a clever title on a new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordinary calls could shrink and take my weekend premium with them. Eight months saved buys some room, but Celia's flower-stall earnings change by season. I could look at hardware counters nearby, though a counter job may pay less than this full week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a tally of warranty calls that require a person to check a hot or leaking appliance. If paid weekend hours actually fall, Celia and I would postpone the planned new sofa and I would compare posted local hardware-counter rotas by full-week wages and hours before applying. In the first year of the change I would keep available paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real pay cut, not terrified. I have savings and shops close enough to ask. I still need the weekly wage to cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you postpone first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the weekend premium disappears, we can sit on the old sofa another year. I won't cancel a household purchase because of a headline alone. The pay slip will tell us when to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which calls still need a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain that a customer saying an oven smells of gas needs a qualified safety response, not a guessing machine. I would follow Vale Home's safety procedure and send the case to the authorised team. The call tally would distinguish that from ordinary part requests.

say: I would warn that **2028 thinking AI** threatens warranty calls before robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues to check **posted paid work**, not hopeful titles.
think: I expect the **warranty queue** and premium to shrink sharply after 2028.
I see eight months saved as **search time**, while other centres may cut together.
do: List **counter and stock jobs** by posted duties, full-week wages, hours and travel; check safe lifting before stock work.
Apply if calls end in 2028-29; accept only **rent-and-bill-covering pay** and hours after travel.
Keep any **remaining paid calls** while using bounded savings for rent.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of the wage supporting household rent.
S2.quote: Eight months saved is time to search, not another wage.
fieldNote: He expects the **weekend premium** to disappear with many calls.
Celia’s stall has **variable receipts**, so he refuses to count a good month as stable pay.
He will not fund **tools or courses** without a real paid opening.

steps.text: List posted paid counter and stock jobs by duties, full-week wages, hours and travel
Apply if calls end in 2028-29; accept only rent-and-bill-covering weekly wages and hours after travel
Keep remaining paid warranty calls while using bounded savings for rent
Check safe stock duties before applying; buy no tools or course without paid opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the warranty headset is in trouble by 2028 because checking a receipt is thinking work. The robots may come around 2031, but their later date does not protect my calls. I would tell younger agents to keep their pay records and look at real vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my calls and weekend premium to go in the first year after 2028. Eight months saved is time to search, not another wage. The other local call centres may be cutting too, and I can't know whether a hardware counter will still need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd list posted paid hardware-counter and parts-desk jobs, checking full-week pay and hours after travel. If my warranty calls end in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a real paid opening, including hands-on stock work if I can do it safely. I'd leave the old rota only when the new weekly wage and hours cover our rent and bills after travel; otherwise I'd keep any paid calls and use a bounded part of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would lose the pay I've built our household around and I'd be awake looking at rent dates. The reserve stops me from freezing, but it doesn't make the job loss small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Celia's stall carry the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Celia's stall can bring in good weeks and empty ones. I would not count an average from one good month as the rent money. We would look at several months of actual receipts before changing my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why consider hands-on stock work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Parts work still has boxes and broken machines in front of you, but robots around 2031 might change that too. I wouldn't buy tools or pay for a course on a guess. I'd first see a paid opening and its duties.

say: I would ask for a **paid stock trial** tied to a real vacancy.
I would support **apprenticeships** for younger workers without claiming a trade is instant.
think: I could test **parts-room work** on paid time before 2031.
I still expect the **warranty queue** to shrink under thinking AI.
do: Try one **paid afternoon** beside the parts clerk if offered.
Count **posted parts-room openings** quarterly; without a suitable vacancy, keep paid calls and compare local counters using bounded savings.
Apply after 2031 closure only if **weekly wages and hours** cover rent and bills after travel.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test the work but no guaranteed paid place.
S3.quote: A paid afternoon will settle more than an advertisement.
fieldNote: He chooses a **supervised paid trial**, not an invented formal course.
He checks **safe lifting** before treating stock work as feasible.
The parts-room plan needs a **real wage and hours** after travel.

steps.text: Keep paid weekend warranty calls while counting posted parts-room openings quarterly
Try one paid parts-room afternoon with clerk if offered and safe lifting is possible
Apply if calls end in 2031-32 only to stock work with rent-and-bill-covering weekly pay/hours after travel
Without suitable parts-room vacancy, keep available paid calls, compare posted counters and bound reserve search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets employers show whether they will pay people to check real appliance faults. I would like the company to keep an apprenticeship route for younger staff, but I won't pretend I can start a trade overnight at sixty. Robots around 2034 make a parts counter no certain shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the physical parts room in ordinary paid shifts before thinking AI reaches my calls in 2031. I still expect my warranty queue to shrink, so the point is to test whether the parts room has a real paid week. I don't need a certificate if a supervisor can show me the stock safely on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask to spend one paid afternoon beside the parts clerk, count the actual openings each quarter, and keep my weekend calls. If the desk still has a paid vacancy, I'd apply for it when calls end in the first year after 2031, but only if its full-week wage and hours cover rent and bills after travel. If there is no suitable place, I'd keep available paid calls and compare other local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can do something before the first cut. Five years gives me time to learn whether I can manage the stock, not a guarantee it will pay enough. I'd sleep better with a real rota in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you physically do the parts-room shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can lift a boxed kettle, but I wouldn't pretend I can move heavy cookers without help. I'd ask the clerk to show me what the shift actually requires. A paid afternoon will settle more than an advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the parts room has no paid opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the warranty rota while it pays and look at posted counter work elsewhere. Celia and I could use part of our reserve for a bounded search. I would not sign away a steady wage for an unpaid trial.

say: I would ask employers for **annual rota plans**.
I would say **2036 thinking AI** reaches calls before 2039 robots affect parts work.
think: I may need **paid shifts at sixty-eight** if verified later income falls short.
I see eight months saved as **search room**, not retirement pay.
do: Keep **weekend warranty calls** while paid and review household figures each autumn.
Compare **posted counter jobs** by full-week pay and hours after travel.
Apply if calls end in 2036-37 only to **paid roles** whose wages and hours cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about unverified later income, with time to plan.
S4.quote: Family supper is not a line of income in our accounts.
fieldNote: He sets an **autumn review** beside the rent renewal to avoid delay.
Celia’s variable **stall receipts** need several months of evidence.
He will not treat grown children as **guaranteed support**.

steps.text: Keep paid warranty shifts and review actual income and rent each autumn
Compare posted counter jobs by full-week wages and hours after travel
Apply if calls end in 2036-37 only for posted bill-covering weekly wages and hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives people time to prepare without pretending every current job lasts. Employers should show honest rota plans each year. Thinking AI reaches the warranty headset by 2036, and hands-on robots may change the parts room around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I might still need paid shifts; we haven't verified any income that would replace mine. Eight months saved gives us room for a search, not a retirement date. I could let the years slip by if I never put our figures on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Celia and I would list actual yearly pay, stall receipts, rent and bills, and request written figures for any income after full-time work. I'd keep the weekend warranty rota while it pays and compare local posted counter jobs each autumn. If calls end in the first year after 2036, I'd apply to a paid position only if complete weekly wages and hours after travel fit our bills; if later-income figures are short, I would keep paid work in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The horizon gives us time to make ordinary plans, but the bills will still arrive. I don't want to assume our grown children or a birthday will settle them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you avoid putting off the figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write it into the same autumn week when we review our rent renewal. If the numbers say I can do fewer weekends, we can choose that. If not, I'll work the paid shifts available and keep the reserve intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a practical skill if they want, but not because I'm asking for their help. They built their own households. Family supper is not a line of income in our accounts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the warranty queue could end before I can replace the weekend wage. A list of genuine paid counter openings and their full-week rotas would help. I would also need a bounded search, not a promise that my children will cover rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the premium hours. A service agent can keep the same title and lose the weekend pay that made the rent work. I would rather hear the true rota than a speech about resilience.

headlineQuote: A service agent can keep the same title and lose the weekend pay that made the rent work.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old** experienced warranty agent with secondary school education.
His **weekend premium** brings higher pay, and he has eight months saved.
He never uses **AI tools** and checks product books for warranty facts.
He favours **paid work** and practical skill over speculative courses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when warranty calls and his weekend premium may disappear quickly.
whatWouldHelp: A list of **posted paid openings** with complete weekly wages and hours.
